title: Test day seven
hookLine: review the week: Zengzi looked back every day, and Confucius told an overthinker that twice may do
tomorrow: why did Moses carry the broken stones too?

lines: SEND IT NOW, OR Version IT AGAIN?
A MINISTER WHO THOUGHT THREE TIMES.
cards: Some people send a text the second they think of it. Others version it in their notes, rewrite it, rewrite it again, and send it the next morning, or never.
Confucius heard about a man like the second kind: Ji Wenzi, a senior minister of Lu from the generation before his, who was known for thinking three times before he acted.
The Analects gives his answer, in James Legge's translation: "Twice may do."

teach.b: So how much looking back is enough? The Analects holds two voices. The first is Zengzi, one of Confucius's students: "I daily examine myself on three points."
Was I faithful to the people I worked for? Was I sincere with my friends? Did I practice what I was taught?
The same honest questions, every day. On this view, review is how a person is formed: you look back steadily, or you drift. The second voice is the Master's own, about Ji Wenzi.
Thinking three times had stopped being wisdom.
The later commentator Zhu Xi read it this way: by the second look, what's right is usually clear, and the third look is where worry and self-interest creep in.
On that view, reviewing can become a place to hide from acting. Zengzi asks you to look back every day. Confucius warns that looking can turn into stalling.
Elsewhere the Analects pictures the noble person as slow to speak and earnest in doing, so in this tradition reflection serves action.
A test week's review can hold both voices: the honest questions, asked once, maybe twice, and then a decision.

how: In the Confucian tradition, self-examination is a daily habit (Analects 1.4), held together with the Master's warning against endless deliberation (5.19). On a personal rule, a test week usually ends with a short written review and one change for the next version.

o: the seventh test day: start the whole rule over from the top
the seventh test day: look back over the week, then decide
the seventh test day: rest, and skip the rule entirely

games.q: two voices in the Analects: tap the pairs.
p: I daily examine myself on three points
a third look lets worry creep in

s: Confucius praised Ji Wenzi for thinking three times before acting
the Analects includes a student who examined himself every day
Zengzi: "I daily examine myself on three points."
one reading of Confucius: after the second look, worry and self-interest creep in.

games.q: you lean toward Confucius: look back lightly, then act. now state Zengzi's side at its strongest.
o: honest questions every day are how a person is formed; skip them and you drift.
thinking three times is always better than thinking twice.
a review only matters after something has gone badly wrong.
games.why: Zengzi's best case: the same honest questions, daily, about faithfulness, sincerity and practice, keep a person true. Confucius didn't drop review; he warned against stalling.

practice: Take a pen and write the week's review in two passes only. First pass: what worked, and what didn't. Second pass: the one change you'll carry into version two, then set the pen down, even if a third pass is tempting.

wordCard.voice: Test day seven: the day you look back over the whole test week, honestly, and then decide. In the Analects, twice may do.

orig.note: classical Chinese, Analects 5.19 (5.20 in some editions): twice, that will do.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: reviewed, twice and then done. Day 1697, and the test week is over.
